strings.d1.theme: Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun
strings.d1.s0.name: Grand Palace Bangkok
strings.d1.s0.tips: The royal palace and the Emerald Buddha (Wat Phra Kaew). Entry is 500 THB, shoulders and knees must be covered. Arrive at 08:30 to beat the crowds.
strings.d1.s1.name: Wat Pho
strings.d1.s1.tips: Home to the 46 m reclining Buddha and the massage school. A 30-minute traditional massage (~300 THB) is available here.
strings.d1.s2.name: Tha Tien Pier
strings.d1.s2.tips: Cross the Chao Phraya on a 5 THB ferry. Wat Arun is right on the other side.
strings.d1.s3.name: Wat Arun
strings.d1.s3.tips: The Temple of Dawn. Climb the steep stairs of the porcelain-covered prang for river views.
strings.d1.s4.name: Supanniga Eating Room Tha Tien
strings.d1.s4.tips: Thai home cooking on the riverside. Have lunch with a view of Wat Arun: moo palo and som tam.
strings.d1.b0.name: Thipsamai Pad Thai
strings.d1.b0.tips: Bangkok's most famous pad thai. Queues build after 17:00, so lunchtime is easier.
strings.d1.b1.name: Museum Siam
strings.d1.b1.tips: An interactive Thai history museum next to Wat Pho. A good option for rainy days.
strings.d2.s0.name: Wat Traimit
strings.d2.s0.tips: Home to the 5.5-tonne golden Buddha. It marks the entrance to Chinatown.
strings.d2.s1.name: Yaowarat Road
strings.d2.s1.tips: Chinatown's main street, with gold shops, temples and quiet side streets by day.
strings.d2.s2.name: Talat Noi
strings.d2.s2.tips: An old Chinese quarter on the riverbank, full of street art, garages and cafés.
strings.d2.s3.name: Hua Seng Hong Yaowarat
strings.d2.s3.tips: A classic Chinatown Chinese restaurant. Order dim sum and goose.
strings.d2.s4.name: Iconsiam
strings.d2.s4.tips: A giant mall across the river. Street food at the Sook Siam floating market floor makes for an air-conditioned afternoon.
strings.d2.b0.name: Nai Ek Roll Noodle
strings.d2.b0.tips: Pork noodle soup on Yaowarat, a street-food classic.
strings.d2.b1.name: Lhong 1919
strings.d2.b1.tips: A restored Chinese temple and warehouse on the riverbank. Calmer than ICONSIAM.
strings.d3.s0.name: Jim Thompson House
strings.d3.s0.tips: A teak Thai house and silk collection. Visits are by guided tour, and the garden is cool.
strings.d3.s1.name: Siam Paragon
strings.d3.s1.tips: Siam's giant mall, with a food market on the lower floor. An air-conditioned break.
strings.d3.s2.name: Som Tam Nua Siam Square
strings.d3.s2.tips: Isan cooking: som tam and fried chicken. The queue moves fast at Siam Square.
strings.d3.s3.name: Erawan Shrine
strings.d3.s3.tips: A Brahma shrine in the middle of the city, with dancers and incense.
strings.d3.s4.name: Lumphini Park
strings.d3.s4.tips: Bangkok's central park, with monitor lizards, sunset and evening aerobics.
strings.d3.b0.name: MBK Center Food Court
strings.d3.b0.tips: The food court on MBK's 6th floor. Cheap and air-conditioned, an alternative to som tam.
strings.d3.b1.name: Benjakitti Park
strings.d3.b1.tips: A new wetland park, and an alternative to Lumphini.
strings.d4.s0.name: Chatuchak Weekend Market
strings.d4.s0.tips: On weekends it is the world's largest market (15,000 stalls). On weekdays, head to the Or Tor Kor food market. Go early, as midday is hot.
strings.d4.s1.name: Or Tor Kor Market
strings.d4.s1.tips: A premium food market next to Chatuchak. Try the mango sticky rice and seafood.
strings.d4.s2.name: Ari Neighbourhood
strings.d4.s2.tips: Bangkok's hipster district, with cafés and boutiques. Take the BTS to Ari.
strings.d4.s3.name: Raan Jay Fai
strings.d4.s3.tips: A Michelin-starred street restaurant. Order the crab omelette (~1,000 THB). Book months ahead, or join the queue at 14:00.
strings.d4.b0.name: Baan Ying Ari
strings.d4.b0.tips: Thai home cooking in Ari. A fallback if Jay Fai doesn't work out.
strings.d4.b1.name: Chatuchak Park
strings.d4.b1.tips: A park next to the market, with shade and a lake.
strings.d5.s0.name: Wat Mahathat Ayutthaya
strings.d5.s0.tips: 1.5 hours from Bangkok by train or minivan. See the Buddha head wrapped in tree roots in this UNESCO-listed ancient capital.
strings.d5.s1.name: Wat Phra Si Sanphet
strings.d5.s1.tips: A royal temple with three chedis, and the symbol of Ayutthaya.
strings.d5.s2.name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
strings.d5.s2.tips: A Khmer-style temple on the riverbank, also famous for its sunset. Go by bicycle.
strings.d5.s3.name: Ayutthaya Boat Noodle
strings.d5.s3.tips: Ayutthaya's boat noodles are served in small bowls. Eat 3 or 4.
strings.d5.s4.name: Ayutthaya Night Market Pier
strings.d5.s4.tips: A riverside market with temple views. The return train leaves at 17:00.
strings.d5.b0.name: Ayutthaya Roti Sai Mai
strings.d5.b0.tips: Cotton candy roti, Ayutthaya's signature sweet.
strings.d5.b1.name: Bang Pa-In Palace
strings.d5.b1.tips: A summer palace on the way back, with gardens and pavilions.
strings.d6.s0.name: Damnoen Saduak Floating Market
strings.d6.s0.tips: 1.5 hours from Bangkok. The famous floating market is quieter at 08:00, and boat hire is negotiable.
strings.d6.s1.name: Maeklong Railway Market
strings.d6.s1.tips: A market set on the railway track. Check the train times (around 11:10 and 14:30).
strings.d6.s2.name: Amphawa Floating Market
strings.d6.s2.tips: A canalside market with grilled seafood served from boats. Livelier at weekends.
strings.d6.s3.name: Wat Bang Kung
strings.d6.s3.tips: A temple swallowed by a banyan tree, near Amphawa.
strings.d6.b0.name: Amphawa Firefly Tour
strings.d6.b0.tips: An evening boat tour (if you stay on) to see fireflies.
strings.d6.b1.name: Damnoen Saduak Boat Food Stall
strings.d6.b1.tips: Noodles and mango served from a boat at the floating market. Choose this if you skip Amphawa.
strings.d7.s0.name: Wat Saket (Golden Mount)
strings.d7.s0.tips: The Golden Mount: 344 steps up to 360° views of the city. Cooler in the morning.
strings.d7.s1.name: Bangkok Flower Market Pak Khlong Talat
strings.d7.s1.tips: A 24-hour flower market, with jasmine garlands and orchids.
strings.d7.s2.name: Baan Khanitha Sathorn
strings.d7.s2.tips: Classic Thai cooking in a Thai house. An air-conditioned farewell lunch.
strings.d7.s3.name: Lumphini MRT / Airport Rail Link
strings.d7.s3.tips: The airport train takes 30 minutes from Phaya Thai. Time to say goodbye.
strings.d7.b0.name: Krua Apsorn Dinso
strings.d7.b0.tips: Home cooking from the royal kitchen tradition. Try the crab omelette.
strings.d7.b1.name: Wat Suthat
strings.d7.b1.tips: A temple with a giant swing. Visit it instead of the Golden Mount.
strings.note0: The BTS Skytrain and MRT are the fastest ways to get around the city. Ask taxis to use the meter, and expect to haggle with touristy tuk-tuks. The Grab app is reliable.
strings.note1: Cover shoulders and knees at temples. Checks are strict at the Grand Palace, where sarongs are sold but pricey.
strings.note2: June to October is the rainy season, with an hour or two of downpour in the afternoon. Sightsee in the morning and save the malls for rain time. Expect 33°C and humidity.
strings.note3: Street food is safe: pick a busy stall, and ice is fine. Pad thai costs 60-100 THB, mango sticky rice 100 THB.
strings.note4: Tipping is not required, and restaurants may add a 10% service charge. Haggling is normal in markets but not in malls.
strings.note5: The train to Ayutthaya from Hua Lamphong takes 1.5 hours (20-60 THB). For the floating markets, take a tour or hire a car.
strings.transit.name: Rabbit Card
strings.transit.why_chosen: Works on the BTS Skytrain. The MRT needs a separate token or card, and both are sold at stations.
